headline: Cramming loses to spacing: the same study time sticks better when spread out.
body: Known as the spacing effect, it's been replicated since Hermann Ebbinghaus's memory experiments in the 1880s. Short reviews over days beat one marathon session.

headline: Quizzing yourself beats rereading your notes.
body: The testing effect: pulling information out of memory strengthens it more than looking at it again. Flashcards and practice questions are doing real work.

headline: In a famous study, about half of viewers missed a person in a gorilla suit.
body: Simons and Chabris (1999) had people count basketball passes. Focused on the count, many never saw the gorilla walk through. It's called inattentional blindness.

headline: You tend to like things more just because you've seen them before.
body: The mere-exposure effect, studied by Robert Zajonc in the 1960s, helps explain why a song grows on you and why brands pay to be everywhere.

headline: A random number you just saw can nudge your next estimate.
body: Anchoring: in Tversky and Kahneman's 1974 work, a spun wheel's number shifted people's guesses about unrelated facts. First offers in negotiations work the same way.

headline: In a list, you remember the first and last items best. The middle gets lost.
body: The serial-position effect: early items get extra rehearsal (primacy) and late ones are still fresh in working memory (recency). Worth knowing before your next presentation.

headline: Divide 72 by your interest rate to see roughly how many years it takes money to double.
body: The Rule of 72: at 8% a year, money doubles in about 9 years. It works for inflation too: at 3%, prices double in about 24 years.

headline: China was using paper money about 1,000 years ago.
body: The jiaozi appeared in Sichuan in the 11th century as a lighter stand-in for heavy iron coins. Merchants issued it first, then the Song government took it over.

headline: On the island of Yap, giant stone discs worked as money without ever moving.
body: Rai stones could be too big to carry, so ownership changed by shared agreement. Everyone just remembered who owned which stone. A ledger, centuries before spreadsheets.

headline: The word "dollar" comes from a silver coin minted in a Bohemian valley.
body: Coins from Joachimsthal were called thalers. The name spread across Europe, became "daler" in Dutch, and was eventually borrowed for the US dollar.

headline: In 1946 Hungary, prices doubled about every 15 hours.
body: It's the worst hyperinflation on record. After WWII, Hungary printed money to cover costs, and the pengő became worthless. The forint replaced it in August 1946.

headline: Your bank deposits in the US are insured up to $250,000 if the bank fails.
body: FDIC coverage applies per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category. The agency was created in 1933 after waves of bank runs during the Great Depression.

headline: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the Great Pyramid's building.
body: The Great Pyramid of Giza went up around 2560 BC. Cleopatra died in 30 BC, about 2,500 years later, and under 2,000 years before Apollo 11 in 1969.

headline: Oxford University was already teaching students before the Aztec capital was founded.
body: There's evidence of teaching at Oxford as early as 1096. Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, was founded in 1325, more than two centuries later.

headline: The Hundred Years' War lasted 116 years.
body: England and France fought on and off from 1337 to 1453, with long truces in between. Historians later grouped the conflicts under one tidy (but inaccurate) name.

headline: Movable type was invented in China about 400 years before Gutenberg's press.
body: Bi Sheng made movable type from baked clay around 1040. Gutenberg's metal type and press in the 1440s were what made mass printing take off in Europe.

headline: Hieroglyphs were cracked thanks to one stone with the same decree in three scripts.
body: The Rosetta Stone carries a 196 BC decree in hieroglyphic, Demotic, and ancient Greek. Using the Greek as a key, Jean-François Champollion announced his breakthrough in 1822.

headline: The Black Death may have killed 30–60% of Europe's population in a few years.
body: The plague swept Europe from 1347 to 1351. The labor shortage that followed pushed up wages and helped loosen the grip of feudalism.

headline: Botanically, bananas are berries and strawberries aren't.
body: A true berry develops from a single flower's ovary with seeds inside. Strawberries carry their seeds on the outside and grow from a swollen base of the flower.

headline: Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood.
body: Two hearts pump blood through the gills and one serves the rest of the body. Their blood uses copper-based hemocyanin instead of iron-based hemoglobin, which makes it blue.

headline: Old church windows aren't thicker at the bottom because glass flows.
body: Glass is an amorphous solid, and at room temperature it doesn't sag over centuries. Old panes were just uneven when made, and installers often put the thick edge down.

headline: A lightning bolt heats the air to about five times hotter than the Sun's surface.
body: The air around a lightning flash can reach about 30,000 °C, while the Sun's surface is roughly 5,500 °C. That sudden heating makes air expand explosively: that's thunder.

headline: Ice floats because water does something weird: it expands when it freezes.
body: Hydrogen bonds lock frozen water into an open crystal about 9% less dense than liquid. So lakes freeze from the top down, and life underneath survives winter.

headline: The "10 bacteria for every human cell" stat is wrong. It's closer to 1:1.
body: A 2016 study recounted and estimated about 38 trillion bacteria and 30 trillion human cells in a typical adult. The old 10:1 figure was a rough guess from the 1970s.

headline: A day on Venus lasts longer than a year on Venus.
body: Venus takes 243 Earth days to spin once, but only 225 Earth days to orbit the Sun. It also spins backward compared with most planets.

headline: The sunlight hitting you right now left the Sun about 8 minutes ago.
body: Light moves at about 300,000 km per second, and the Sun is about 150 million km away. If the Sun vanished, you wouldn't know for roughly 8 minutes.

headline: Saturn is less dense than water.
body: It's the only planet in our solar system with an average density below water's, because it's mostly hydrogen and helium. NASA jokes it could float in a big enough bathtub.

headline: Astronauts on the ISS see about 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every day.
body: The International Space Station circles Earth roughly every 90 minutes at around 28,000 km/h. That's a lot of sunrises to sleep through.

headline: Olympus Mons on Mars is about 2.5 times taller than Mount Everest.
body: It rises more than 21 km. Mars has no moving tectonic plates, so lava kept piling up over the same hotspot for ages, and lower gravity let the volcano grow huge.

headline: When you see the Andromeda Galaxy, you're seeing light that left it 2.5 million years ago.
body: At about 2.5 million light-years away, it's one of the most distant things you can see with the naked eye. That light set out before modern humans existed.

headline: The WHO recommends at least 150 minutes of moderate exercise a week.
body: That's about 30 minutes, five days a week, of things like brisk walking. The WHO estimates about 1 in 3 adults worldwide don't hit that bar.

headline: Your heart beats roughly 100,000 times a day.
body: At a resting rate of around 70 beats a minute, that adds up fast: about 36 million beats a year, without you ever having to think about it.

headline: Babies are born with more bones than adults.
body: Newborns have around 270 bones, many partly made of cartilage. As they grow, several fuse together, leaving the 206 bones of a typical adult skeleton.

headline: Tooth enamel is the hardest substance in your body.
body: It's about 96% mineral. The catch: enamel has no living cells, so once acid or decay wears it away, your body can't grow it back.

headline: Caffeine's half-life is several hours, so that 4 p.m. coffee is still with you at bedtime.
body: In healthy adults, it takes roughly 3 to 7 hours for your body to clear half of the caffeine you drank. Genetics, pregnancy, and smoking all change the speed.

headline: Measles can erase part of your immune system's memory of other diseases.
body: Called immune amnesia, the virus destroys memory cells that protected you from past infections. It's one reason measles vaccination saves more lives than the numbers first suggest.

headline: The Pomodoro Technique is named after a tomato-shaped kitchen timer.
body: Francesco Cirillo came up with it as a university student in the late 1980s: work in 25-minute bursts, then take a short break. "Pomodoro" is Italian for tomato.

headline: "Work expands to fill the time available" started as a joke in The Economist.
body: C. Northcote Parkinson opened a 1955 satirical essay about growing bureaucracies with that line. It's now Parkinson's law, and a solid argument for tighter deadlines.

headline: The 80/20 rule started with an economist noticing who owned land in Italy.
body: Vilfredo Pareto observed that about 80% of Italy's land belonged to 20% of the people. Management thinker Joseph Juran later turned it into a general rule of thumb.

headline: Henry Ford helped make the 40-hour, five-day workweek normal back in 1926.
body: Ford Motor Company moved factory workers to five 8-hour days without cutting pay. Part of the bet: workers with free time would also become customers.

headline: Switching between tasks has a hidden cost, even when each switch feels instant.
body: Research on task switching shows your brain needs time to drop one set of rules and load another. Frequent switching slows you down and increases errors.

headline: People underestimate how long tasks take, even when they know past ones ran late.
body: It's called the planning fallacy. We picture the best-case path and ignore our own track record. A fix: base estimates on how long similar projects actually took.

headline: In 1947, engineers found a real moth stuck in a computer and taped it into the logbook.
body: Grace Hopper's team on the Harvard Mark II noted the "first actual case of bug being found." Engineers already used "bug" for glitches, but the moth made it famous.

headline: The world's first website is still online.
body: Tim Berners-Lee put info.cern.ch live at CERN in 1991. It explained what the World Wide Web was and how to use it, and you can still visit it today.

headline: The computer that guided Apollo to the Moon had about 4 KB of RAM.
body: The Apollo Guidance Computer had 2,048 words of erasable memory. Its programs were woven by hand into rope memory, with wires passing through or around tiny magnetic cores.

headline: Bluetooth is named after a Viking-age Danish king.
body: Harald "Bluetooth" Gormsson united parts of Denmark and Norway, like the tech unites devices. The logo combines the runes for his initials, H and B.

headline: Ada Lovelace published a program for a computer that was never built, in 1843.
body: Her notes on Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine included a step-by-step method for computing Bernoulli numbers. She also guessed machines could one day work with music, not just math.

headline: British spies invented public-key encryption years before it was "invented" in public.
body: At GCHQ, Clifford Cocks came up with a scheme like RSA in 1973, years before RSA was published in 1977. It stayed classified until 1997.
